speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how will the revised wages for the cleaning sector under the Progressive Wage Model impact the wages of other lower wage workers; (b) what are the future plans for sectors with lower wage workers; and (c) how will this build a stronger social compact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Manpower with the adjustments to cleaners’ wages under the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) (a) what will be the overall increase in costs to the industry in a year given the additional manpower required due to the COVID-19 pandemic; (b) how will businesses and the community be impacted by such additional costs; and (c) how is the Ministry engaging the industry to increase mechanisation to raise productivity and cut manpower needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what are the roll-out plans for the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for the retail and food services sector; (b) what is the plan to implement PWM for other vocational roles that are not currently covered under the PWM; and (c) how will PWM contribute to shifting away from reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how is the wage ladder under the latest Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for the cleaning sector decided upon; and (b) whether the Government will provide support to cleaning companies with existing contracts that are tendered based on the previous PWM wage recommendation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower in the past decade, how does growth in the wages of the bottom 20% of workers compare with (i) median wage growth in Singapore and (ii) income growth of bottom 20% of workers in OECD countries.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how has the COVID-19 pandemic affected lower wage workers; and (b) whether the pandemic has delayed implementation timelines for expansion of the Progressive Wage Model to other sectors and other efforts to uplift lower wage workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower whether the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) will be adjusted such that enhancements to wages under the Progressive Wage Model are not entirely offset by lower WIS payouts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether the Tripartite Cluster for Cleaners (TCC) discussed ways to ensure that the higher cost arising from enhanced wages under the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for the cleaning sector will be fairly borne by cleaning companies, service buyers and the public, (b) what are some of the feedback the TCC received from cleaning companies and their service buyers; and (c) what lessons can be drawn from this as the PWM is expanded to other sectors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: asked the Minister for Manpower given plans to adopt a vocational approach for the Progressive Wage Model (PWM), how will progressive wages be extended to workers who are employed by companies in sectors not currently covered by the PWMs and whose majority of rank and file workers will not be on PWM, without disrupting the pay and cost structure in such companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: asked the Minister for Manpower how will the cleaning industry be impacted by the recent announcement on the Progressive Wage Model for cleaners.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what has been the average wage increase of cleaners under the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) over the years; (b) whether the PWM has improved the quality of cleaning; (c) whether the PWM has caused a reduction in the number of cleaners employed, especially for those smaller scale F&B outlets; and (d) whether the PWM has a knock-on effect on food prices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Manpower whether the income qualifying criteria for Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) will be adjusted in line with the new Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: asked the Minister for Manpower how will Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) complement the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) so that an increase in wages of workers through PWM is not offset by a reduction in WIS payouts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our fundamental objective is to make sure that as a society, we take care of every worker.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We cannot progress as a society and achieve economic progress with a strong social compact if there is a group of workers who are left behind.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must ensure that every worker who is prepared to work hard will be able to earn fair wages and prosper along with the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Uplifting our low-wage workers has been a priority for the Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Introduced in 2007, Workfare is the foundation of the Government's support for low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It supplements the incomes of our low-wage workers in cash and helps them save for retirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This encourages them to work regularly, rather than rely on welfare measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Studies have shown that Workfare has led to an increase in employment rates, with the highest increases among our older workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare also supports our lower wage workers to upskill themselves, increase their productivity, find better jobs and earn higher wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Another $600 million has been paid out to employers and workers through the Workfare Skills Support Scheme, to enhance their skills and employability.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On top of Workfare, the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) provides job and training progression pathways for our lower wage workers, to grow their wages as they improve their skills and productivity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our policies to support our low-wage workers have made a difference in uplifting them, helping them to enjoy good wage growth over the last decade.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This has allowed our low-wage workers to gain ground and progress faster than the median.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That means the low-wage workers are earning closer to the median wage.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While we see robust real income growth for them, this is not the case for most OECD countries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, over the same 10-year period, workers at the 20th percentile in the United Kingdom saw no real wage growth, while those in Japan and United States saw only cumulative real wage growth of 3% and 6% respectively, despite having minimum wage.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Nonetheless, we should not take our progress for granted.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is not inevitable that this will always be so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: After taking this into account, the incomes of the first 20% of income earners in 2020 were actually similar to wages in 2019.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As we helped our low-wage workers cope with COVID-19, it was also timely that we look to strengthen their prospects and progression for the long term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is why we formed the Tripartite Workgroup on Lower-Wage Workers last year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Workgroup will be releasing its recommendations in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government's aspiration remains to cover all sectors with Progressive Wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Workgroup has already announced that it will introduce PWMs in three new sectors: food services, retail and waste management.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Workgroup is also looking at introducing Progressive Wages to other low-wage occupations that straddle multiple sectors, as raised by Miss Rachel Ong.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Agreeing which sector should start the PWM is just the first step.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The hard work of making sure that it achieves its objective of progress for low-wage workers and sustaining high employment is in the details.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are carefully negotiated by the tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: When it was first introduced in 2012, the mindsets of employers and service buyers were different.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Much effort went into getting their support and their buy-in.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There were concerns whether wage increases were sustainable, whether they would lead to higher costs for essential services in our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But today, all our PWM stakeholders buy into the same vision and work together to support our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers now better understand the benefits of PWM to them and to their workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This win-win outcome is why the cleaning sector has been able to agree to a much more ambitious rate of growth in its most recently concluded run of review.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To Ms Hany Soh's question, cleaners' wages have risen by 26% cumulatively from 2014 to 2019 and we have seen local employment rise by 3%.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Overall, while businesses have had to adjust to the wage increases, they have had been able to do so without adverse effect.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked how they will impact wages of other low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For related jobs, there could potentially be some positive spillover effects.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Nonetheless, if we want to achieve more broad-based progress for more low-wage workers, more of them would have to be brought in directly into our Progressive Wage system.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Hence, the Tripartite Workgroup's discussion to include more sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some Members, including Mr Gan Thiam Poh, wanted more information of how future wage increases for the cleaning sector were determined.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Hence, the representatives from the cleaning sector are part of the Tripartite Cluster for Cleaners (TCC), which negotiated the wage increases.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The TCC, which oversees the cleaning PWM, consists of representatives from the unions, employers, service buyers, as well as the Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The TCC consulted widely with the industry and had numerous vigorous discussions amongst its members to find common ground that benefits all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is the uniqueness of Singapore's approach because PWM progression is brought about with tripartite consensus.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Edward Chia and Mr Sharael Taha asked about the lessons drawn from our experience with the cleaning PWM.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: A key takeaway is that the negotiated approach of the PWM helps address concerns and allows the sector to raise wages at a pace that is suitable for them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The robust wage increases for the cleaning PWM are fruits of almost a decade of close tripartite collaboration and consistent efforts of the TCC.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The TCC has learned over time to harness the PWM design to benefit their workers and the sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Cleaning companies recognise that Singapore's resident workforce is ageing.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And that in addition to better wages, they needed to re-design the jobs to better retain and attract workers to the sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Their support also assures us that the wage increases are sustainable.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Through negotiation, the PWM allows stakeholders to take sector-specific circumstances into account.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One example is the six-year wage schedule as highlighted by Ms Yeo Wan Ling.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The TCC did so to provide employees and service providers with clarity for long-term planning.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Cleaning firms can price in the wage increases in their multi-year contracts with service buyers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is also a midpoint review so that the TCC can ensure that the wage increases remain sustainable.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This pandemic has showed us how the PWM approach is superior to a blunt minimum wage.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The sectoral approach has enabled us to advance PWM for cleaners as well as other sectors that are able to adjust to PWM progression in the short term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: A blunt minimum wage may not have been able to achieve consensus or as ambitious a wage growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Sectors such as tourism, aviation, hospitality and others that were severely impacted by COVID-19 would not have been able to agree to such a move.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, our targeted approach enabled the tripartite movement to advance PWM at a pace depending on how different sectors perform in the market.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The tripartite clusters for the new sectors such as food services and retail will similarly take into account market conditions and what each sector can manage as they recover from the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng would be happy to know that these sectors are making good headway in developing their PWMs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The cleaning PWM is also not pursuing wage increases without considering skills, productivity and industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This ensures that our workers continue to be upskilled and helps reduce the sector's reliance on low value-added manpower, including foreign manpower as raised by Mr Yip.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Members have raised questions on how businesses and consumers will handle the additional costs and also how productivity in the sector can be increased.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Indeed, if we as a society would like to see low-wage workers make good progress sustainably, all of us have a role to play in this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers have to drive productivity improvements in their firms through better technology and processes as raised by Mr Don Wee.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They may also have to explore new business models or services to value-add to their customers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Service buyers have to embrace outcome-based contracting and contract durations that encourage investments in new technology.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are indeed directions that the industry has articulated in the Industry Transformation Map for the environmental services sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Consumers will also contribute by sharing the cost of wage increases and have to pay slightly more for services and products as the sector implements the PWM.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about how the Government will increase productivity in the cleaning sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Productivity growth is a result of workers and firms working together to grow the business and then fairly redistribute the fruits of growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is why the tripartite movement believe that the Progressive Wage Model is better than a blunt minimum wage.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is something that the Tripartite Workgroup is looking at as part of its deliberations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Ministry of Manpower has been reviewing and enhancing Workfare with significant improvements made recently in 2017 and 2020.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At each review, the wage growth of our low-wage workers has been taken into consideration and qualifying criteria adjusted accordingly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government will continue to review Workfare regularly to ensure that low-wage workers remain adequately supported.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government and tripartite partners are working closely together to make progressive wages a reality for all sectors of our economy sooner rather than later.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I urge this House and all Singaporeans to support our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Keep your supplementary questions short and limit to just one.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is without a doubt that we must uplift our lower wage workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, I am concerned about the impact on our smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What can be done to assist our smaller businesses in business transformation to cope as an employer and as a service buyer?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the one hand, you want wages to go up but you do not want workers to lose their jobs either if the company closes down or the company says, "I cannot afford this", and they have to let go of workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One, over time, this is why we find it very important, and I support the NTUC's work in this too, with the Company Training Committees, because these are important aspects which we want to help companies to look at – job re-design, productivity enhancements – and how they can leverage Government schemes with Enterprise Singapore providing the Productivity Solutions Grant and other development grants that they can use.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are areas in which the Government intends to provide support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement would like to extend our support for the PWM.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Of course, central to the Labour Movement has always been the issue of unemployment as we raise wages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State, what are the safeguards that we can put in place to make sure that as we journey to the next milestone for PWM, we do not create undue unemployment?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think that is one way in which we ensure that our workers are not left behind or disemployed, fully understanding the risk that for many of our low-wage workers, the profile of this group is really the older groups, the less skilled.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We know that these are also the ones who are most at risk with disemployment effects.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On one hand, I think this is where tripartite consensus will have to move ahead as we embark on putting more sectors on board.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And that is why we have been talking to companies, employers to see how this would impact them, and how their views are in the way forward and the years ahead, whether they can absorb some of these wage increases and how much we can pass on to consumers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I also want to say that consumers, too, have their part to play, in terms of supporting these initiatives and efforts, to pay more for services and products to support our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have also seen how companies have transformed to put in place more mechanisation, different ways of cleaning, more clean technology being put in place, and more being explored.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I know NTUC and the cleaning sector are also working to see how they can improve not just the conditions of work, but also the methods in which we re-design our cleaning sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think most importantly is this, that productivity level is not just viewed from the workers' angle.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the end of the day, there is only so much floor you can clean and so many roads you can sweep.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I think, ultimately, for many companies involved, not just the cleaning sector, but others, that you have to look at productivity at both the employee level and the enterprise level.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is why the whole enterprise transformation, job re-design becomes an important factor in this because then you can see the multiples in terms of productivity increases over time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The security sector has done very well with this: moving into technology, sensors, CCTVs and so forth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And that is where we want to move many more of our sectors into, so that we can target better wage increases.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It becomes more sustainable because productivity as a whole, for the whole sector, improves over time.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the planning for the roll-out of the Progressive Wage Model (PWM), does the Ministry take into account job types that may become obsolete or face disruptions in the next five to 10 years?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And in such circumstances, what measures would the Ministry take to ensure that the livelihoods of our workers, particularly those in the lower paying tiers, are not affected?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As a whole, as I have shared, many of the employers are very supportive of our PWM moves.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think they are also in line with us in our ambition to expand progressive wages and, at the same time, to try to grow this closer to median or to increase wages past the median.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: More importantly, as wages go up, workers must also do their part to train, upskill, become relevant and address some of these new opportunities that come by.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Yes, with or without PWM, there may be transformations within each sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have got to look at it quite closely.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ultimately, we will do our best to be the catch-all too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If there are any displaced, to try to match them and move them into sectors that will absorb them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Question Nos 58-59 and 86 have been postponed to the sitting of Parliament on 26 July 2021.]
